$comment: Purchasing-power-adjusted price policy for GeoSpoof IAPs and subscriptions.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS: base_storefront is United States and every other
territory currently uses Apple's automated equalized price. That is
arithmetically correct but ignores purchasing power entirely — $2.99/month
is a very different ask in Jakarta than in Stockholm.
READ BEFORE APPLYING — two consequences that are easy to miss:
1. Manually pricing a territory OPTS IT OUT of Apple's automatic FX and tax
equalization, permanently, until someone edits it again. Apple: 'Prices
also won't change on the storefronts where you manually manage prices
instead of using the automated equalized prices.'
https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=wim4cztw
This trades Apple maintaining your prices for you against controlling
them yourself. Currency moves become your problem. Accepted deliberately.
2. Subscription price INCREASES in Austria, Germany and Poland require every
affected subscriber to actively consent (since 2025-08-04); non-consenting
subscribers are chased weekly and churn at cycle end. Elsewhere
size/velocity criteria still apply. Decreases never require consent.
Hence allow_increases: false — the planner refuses to emit an increase.
ON THE TIER LISTS BELOW: these are World Bank income groups applied by hand
and are the least trustworthy part of this file. Classifications shift, and
several countries here sit near a boundary (see needs_review). Do not treat
them as authoritative. The planner reconciles against Apple's live territory
list from /v1/territories and reports anything unclassified rather than
guessing, so gaps surface as output instead of as silent mispricing.
The multipliers are a BUSINESS DECISION. 1.0/0.6/0.4/0.3 is a conventional
indie starting point, not a recommendation.
$allow_increases_comment: Split by product type, because the risk is not symmetric.
One-time purchases (pro.lifetime, the three tips) have no existing subscribers
to consent, so raising them in high-purchasing-power markets is safe and is
where the observed upside actually lives.
Subscriptions are the opposite. Increases in Austria, Germany and Poland
require every affected subscriber to actively consent (since 2025-08-04) or
they churn at cycle end; elsewhere Apple's size/velocity criteria may still
demand consent. So monthly/annual are decrease-only until you decide the
churn risk is worth it. Adapty's index shows real-world spread of +62% to
-63% versus US, so leaving subscription upside on the table is a real cost —
it is just not one to take by accident.
$rounding_comment: 'nearest' picks the closest available price point in either direction.
This is not cosmetic. A lower-middle monthly target of $1.20 against points
[0.99, 1.49] snaps down to 0.99 either way, but a low-income lifetime target
of $7.50 against [6.99, 7.99] snaps UP to 7.99 under 'nearest', because 0.49
is nearer than 0.51 — giving back part of the discount. 'down' would pick
6.99. Choose deliberately: 'nearest' is balanced, 'down' guarantees the
discount is never partially undone but costs proceeds on every rounding.
$tie_break_comment: When two available price points are equally far from the target AND share an
equally attractive ending, this decides which wins. Ties are common: target
8.99 against points [7.99, 9.99] is exactly equidistant and both end in .99.
'cheaper' errs toward the discount this whole exercise is meant to deliver;
'dearer' protects proceeds. Stated explicitly because otherwise the outcome
is whatever the sort happens to reach first, which is nobody's decision.

$comment: DOCUMENTATION ONLY — the planner does not scale from these. Recorded so a
reader knows what the US base is without opening App Store Connect.
The planner's baseline is the product's CURRENT price in each territory,
which is Apple's automated equalized price: already in the right currency
with FX and tax applied. Scaling a USD figure would be wrong, because price
points are denominated locally — a USD target of 1.79 is below every
Brazilian price point, so a nearest-match would pin Brazil to Apple's
cheapest BRL point. Using the local price as the baseline needs no exchange
rates at all, since Apple's ladder already encodes them.
Applied to the territory's CURRENT local price, then snapped to the nearest
available Apple price point in that same currency.
Expect the realised discount to differ from the multiplier, sometimes a lot.
Ladders are coarse at low prices: a Japanese target of ¥240 sits between the
¥200 and ¥300 points and snaps to ¥200, which is -50% rather than the -40%
asked for. Korea and India behave similarly. The plan CSV reports delta_pct
per row so the realised figure is visible before anything is applied.
Per-country coefficients, which is what apps operating at scale actually use
— Steam, Spotify and Netflix all price per country rather than by income
band. Income tiers are a decent default but demonstrably wrong in specific
markets, so override those rather than distorting a whole tier.
Sourced from published practice and benchmarks, NOT measured from your own
data, and therefore starting points rather than answers:
India 0.30, Brazil 0.45, Switzerland 1.10 per
https://github.com/iosdevmax/ppp-pricing
Emerging markets generally 30-60% of US per
https://mwm.ai/glossary/price-localization
Annual-plan spread reaches 4.4x between Germany and Turkey per Adapty,
which implies Turkey nearer 0.25 than the 0.5 its income tier would give.
https://adapty.io/blog/health-fitness-app-subscription-benchmarks/
Values above 1.0 only take effect where the product type permits increases
(see allow_increases_*). Nordics and Switzerland sustain above-US pricing;
that upside is capturable today on lifetime and tips, not on subscriptions.

needs_review.$comment: Territories I am least confident about, either because they recently changed World Bank group or because they sit close to a boundary. Verify these before the first apply; a wrong tier here is a real mispricing, not a rounding error.

territory_overrides.$comment: Explicit per-territory target prices in that territory's own currency, bypassing the tier multiplier. Use where you know the psychologically right number. Still snapped to the nearest available Apple price point.

$comment: Preference order when several points sit equally close to the target. Apple's
ladder already skews to local conventions, so this mostly breaks ties.
Lookup order is territory, then CURRENCY, then default — currency is the
right granularity for most of this, since every euro-zone storefront shares
the .99 convention and every yen price is a whole number. Territory keys are
for genuine one-offs.

$unclassified_rationale: The ~20 territories still unclassified are left on Apple's automated price
Most are high-income (Macau, Brunei, Bermuda, Cayman, the smaller Caribbean
storefronts, Seychelles). Classifying them as high_income would apply a
multiplier of 1.0 and change no price at all — pure busywork with ongoing
maintenance cost, since a manually-priced territory stops receiving Apple's
Venezuela is excluded deliberately rather than for lack of confidence:
hyperinflation means any fixed local price ages badly, and Apple's automated
equalization handles that better than a number frozen in this file.
The principle: classify a market when you have volume or confidence in it.
A wrong tier is worse than Apple's equalized price.
